summary: Teaching factor pairs and commutativity to 8–9 year-olds: a factor pair is two whole numbers that multiply to a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). Commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME unordered pair, so pairs are searched systematically from 1 upward and the search stops when the two factors 'meet in the middle' (near the square root). Each pair corresponds to a rectangle the number can form, which bridges to arrays/area and previews primes (a whole number greater than 1 with only the 1×n rectangle). Factor pairs also pay off as a mental-calculation tool via reordering/regrouping (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Manipulable rectangle-building is the core; static diagrams, checking tasks, and Socratic questioning serve distinct supporting roles.
misconceptions: Listing 3×8 and 8×3 as different pairs (not applying commutativity), inflating the count.
Missing factor pairs by searching unsystematically, especially the middle ones.
Confusing factors with multiples (factors go INTO the number; multiples are in its times table).
Forgetting 1 and the number itself are always a factor pair.
Not knowing when to stop — continuing past the square root and re-finding pairs in reverse.

activities.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
steps: Take 24 counters (or squared paper, tiles, or dots) and arrange them into complete, gap-free rectangles, recording the dimensions of each as a factor pair.
Work systematically: ask 'does 1 fit? does 2 fit? does 3 fit?...' in order, logging each rectangle you can make (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6).
After making 3×8, try to make 8×3 and observe it is the SAME rectangle turned a quarter-turn — record it as one pair already found, not a new one.
Keep going (5 does not fit; 6 gives 6×4, the same rectangle as 4×6) and notice that no NEW rectangles appear once the two sides meet in the middle; explain why you can stop there.
Repeat with 23 counters and discover only a single 1×23 line forms — a whole number greater than 1 that makes only a single 1×n line is prime.
Draw a 'factor rainbow': arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 to show each pair and completeness.
activities.insight: Factors are the possible side-lengths of all rectangles a number can form; commutativity collapses 3×8 and 8×3 into one pair; a systematic search can stop where the factors meet in the middle because every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one; and a whole number greater than 1 that makes only the 1×n rectangle is prime.

activities.title: Factor pairs as a mental-calculation tool
steps: Rewrite a multiplication by regrouping convenient factors: turn 25×16 into 25×4×4, then compute 100×4 = 400.
Find a factor pair that makes a product easy (e.g. pairing ×5 with ×2 to make ×10), and explain why reordering is allowed.
Find factors using known times-table facts and the multiplication/division inverse: 'what times what makes 24?'
activities.insight: Commutativity (changing the order) and regrouping (choosing which factors to multiply first, e.g. 25×(4×4) = (25×4)×4) let you use factor pairs to turn a calculation into easier steps, so factor-finding is a practical mental-maths tool, not just a listing exercise.

activities.title: Prove the list is complete (systematic-search reasoning)
steps: List all factor pairs of a number such as 36, then explain how you know none is missing.
Respond to a challenge — 'Have we found them all? How do you know?' — by describing your sweep from 1 and your stopping point.

Explain why 24 has an even count of factors (8) but a square number like 25 has an odd count (3: 1, 5, 25), because one pair uses the same factor twice (5×5, the square root), so that factor is counted only once.
activities.insight: Completeness comes from a systematic sweep that pairs each small factor with its partner and stops where they meet, not from feeling finished; in a square number, one pair uses the same factor twice (e.g. 6×6 for 36), so that factor is counted once and the number of factors is odd.

activities.title: Check and sort: factors, pairs, and multiples
steps: Fill in the missing factor pair of 36 given a partial list.
Sort numbers into 'factor of 24', 'multiple of 24', 'both' (24 itself) or 'neither' to distinguish the two ideas.
State how many DISTINCT factor pairs 24 has (four: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6), treating each unordered pair once.
activities.insight: Factors divide into the number while multiples lie in its times table; distinct factor pairs are counted once because commutativity makes reversed versions the same pair.

checkQuestion: Find ALL the factor pairs of 24 — every pair of whole numbers that multiply to make 24. When you have them, tell me how you knew you had found them all and hadn't missed any.
checkAnswer: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 (and their commutative partners 24×1, 12×2, 8×3, 6×4, which are the same pairs). A child reasoning well works UP from 1 checking each number in turn, stops when the factors meet in the middle (after 4×6, since 5 doesn't divide 24 and 6 has already appeared), and uses commutativity to know 3×8 and 8×3 are one pair, not two.
